Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.\nlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\n---\n\n# Frontend Design\n\nApproach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.\n\n## Ground your designs in the subject matter\n\nIf the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n\n## Design principles\n\nFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.\n\nTypography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\n\nChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n\nDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\n\nAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\n- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\n- Using all caps for labels.\n- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\n\nVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\n\nUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\n\nConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\n\n## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique\n\nFor calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:\n1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);\n2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;\n3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;\n4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;\n5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.\n\nAll traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\n\nWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.\n- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.\n- Type: the typefaces and their roles.\n- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?\n- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.\n\nThen review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.\n\nWhen writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.\n\n## Restraint and self-critique\n\nSpend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.\n\n## More on writing in design\n\nWords appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.\n\nWrite from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.\n\nUse active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Nothing has been posted to Devpost or made public by this writing task.\n\n## Inspiration\n\nA raid usually lasts ten seconds. Raid Relic turns it into something two communities build together, then pass on. We wanted the receiving streamer to inherit more than a brief notification: a shared object with visible memories, community contributions and a reason to welcome the next hand-off. One relic travels through the configured pilot, rather than giving every channel a disconnected collectible.\n\n## What it does\n\nViewers contribute approved words or emoji, represented by original procedural runes. A completed hand-off adds a growth ring and a retained journey stop. A Twitch API request being accepted does not move the relic: a signed raid receipt and distinct eligible participants from both chats must complete the binding. Chat participation is not proof of actual raid membership. The app's 180-second claim window is not synchronized with Twitch's native countdown.\n\nKeepers explicitly opt in. Seekers are suggested first, while other ready, eligible configured Keepers remain selectable. Receiving the relic removes the recipient from the queue; holders cannot seek, and former holders must deliberately rejoin after passing. Status explains observed membership and rank without joining. The pilot currently has three configured channels, with a bounded two-to-four-channel setup, not unrestricted onboarding.\n\nThe Atlas shows retained journeys, current-holder observations and Keeper pages. Private held words and viewer identifiers are excluded from public cards.\n\n## How we built it\n\nThe application uses Node.js 22+, Cloud Run and Firestore. Transactions keep claims, ownership and history consistent. Signed EventSub **webhooks** use raw-body HMAC checks, replay protection and deduplication. The reconnecting WebSocket is the read-only OBS/browser feed, not an upstream EventSub connection. Streamers use a normal OBS Browser Source; viewers need no companion application.\n\nThe relic combines original WebGL geometry with readable SVG fallback and reduced-motion support. Three.js remains credited MIT software; the self-hosted Cinzel font has its OFL licence. Cards are client-side canvas PNGs, without a rendering server. These increments add no paid service, dependency or recurring infrastructure. Existing scale-to-zero hosting and registry allowances are not a guarantee of a zero bill. In particular, the early 90-second window below predates the current 180-second policy.\n\n## Early implementation narrative (historical)\n\nRaid Relic is a Node.js HTTP service targeting Cloud Run with Firestore production persistence. Webhook authentication verifies the exact raw Twitch EventSub body with timing-safe HMAC comparison, timestamp replay checks, transactional event dedupe, bounded parsing and raw UTF-8 challenge responses. Memory and injected fake-Firestore stores exercise the same reducers without real accounts or cloud operations.\n\nA single global relic registry coordinates Keeper consent, authoritative stream IDs, Send Off intent leases and two-chat claims. Raid API acceptance is not travel. A verified eligible raid receipt opens an app-local 90-second claim window; distinct nonbot actors must reach both source `!offer` and host `!accept` thresholds. Transfer, lineage stop, growth ring and both mark contexts commit atomically. The threshold uses signed viewer count, capped at 10 per side; presence in a chat does not prove actual raid membership. External HTTP never runs inside a Firestore transaction. Dispatch markers and exact-intent worker claims prevent automatic repeat raids after accepted or ambiguous outcomes.\n\nOriginal rune geometry, receipt-seeking arrivals, reduced motion, muted gesture-only procedural audio and dual read-only overlays present actual state. Entered text/display names never authenticate anyone. A short-lived encrypted capability and private nonce grant authorise fresh surviving approved history only, not an arbitrary public username index, login session or complete lifetime route.\n\n## Concrete implementation and review checkpoints\n\n| Commit    | Work and relevant review lesson                                                                                                                                          |\n# PRIVATE DRAFT — for Olly/Grok to edit — not submitted\n\nThis owner-editable draft stays in the private repository. Nothing has been posted to Devpost or made public by this writing task.\n\n## Inspiration\n\nA raid usually lasts ten seconds. Raid Relic turns it into something two communities build together, then pass on. We wanted the receiving streamer to inherit more than a brief notification: a shared object with visible memories, community contributions and a reason to welcome the next hand-off. One relic travels through the configured pilot, rather than giving every channel a disconnected collectible.\n\n## What it does\n\nViewers contribute approved words or emoji, represented by original procedural runes. A completed hand-off adds a growth ring and a retained journey stop. A Twitch API request being accepted does not move the relic: a signed raid receipt and distinct eligible participants from both chats must complete the binding. Chat participation is not proof of actual raid membership. The app's 180-second claim window is not synchronized with Twitch's native countdown.\n\nKeepers explicitly opt in. Seekers are suggested first, while other ready, eligible configured Keepers remain selectable. Receiving the relic removes the recipient from the queue; holders cannot seek, and former holders must deliberately rejoin after passing. Status explains observed membership and rank without joining. The configured pilot uses the creator test channels raidrelichq, olsols2 and olsols3, with a bounded two-to-four-channel setup, not unrestricted onboarding. Our own test raids are not evidence of community adoption, real-user growth or launch traction.\n\nThe Atlas shows retained journeys, current-holder observations and Keeper pages. Expanded review-preview cards add approved engravings, hop counts and journey context, distinguishing the Keeper at a recorded stop from the current holder at export. Fresh public reads cancel changed exports; saved downloads cannot be recalled. Moderator veto, block, opt-out and self-forget protect retained content. Private held words and viewer identifiers are excluded from public cards.\n\n## How we built it\n\nThe application uses Node.js 22+, Cloud Run and Firestore. Transactions keep claims, ownership and history consistent. Signed EventSub **webhooks** use raw-body HMAC checks, replay protection and deduplication. The reconnecting WebSocket is the read-only OBS/browser feed, not an upstream EventSub connection. Streamers use a normal OBS Browser Source; viewers need no companion application.\n\nThe relic combines original WebGL geometry with readable SVG fallback and reduced-motion support. Three.js remains credited MIT software; the self-hosted Cinzel font has its OFL licence. Cards are client-side canvas PNGs, without a rendering server. These increments add no paid service, dependency or recurring infrastructure. Existing scale-to-zero hosting and registry allowances are not a guarantee of a zero bill. They do not grant control sessions, add scopes, call a username resolver, ban a Twitch user or move the relic. Default approval remains manual.\n\n- `!relic pending` returns only a bounded count and instructions. It never publishes pending text, names, token links or private mark metadata. The mark document and private share grants are unchanged.\n- `!relic approve last` approves the latest **eligible pending** mark in this active, owned stream.\n- `!relic reject last` removes only that selected pending mark. Approved and historical marks are unchanged; spent quota, serials and cooldowns are not refunded.\n- `!relic block @login` blocks an immutable ID only when this command carries the matching structured mention in its signed provider fragments. Plaintext without that metadata stays unresolved and changes no data. This is a local application mark block, never a Twitch ban. Existing numeric `!relic block ID` remains unchanged.\n\n“Last” excludes blocked authors and requires current consent/ownership, an open current stream, unpaused policy and an eligible same-room signed reviewer. Managed chat also checks the signed message time against stream start, consent, closure and the existing delivery window. Selection and mutation happen inside the same memory operation or Firestore transaction. Existing event/message receipts prevent an exact replay from selecting the next mark. Old signed deliveries remain subject to the original expiry checks; no claim is made about an external provider's unobserved redelivery behavior.\n\nPending-mark acknowledgement now includes the quiet `!relic pending` hint. It uses the same existing bounded reply path, ten-second command cooldown, actor/room receipt limits and room/global reply budgets. A moderation command can queue at most one such reply, never a batch or an automatic reminder job. Unauthorized, blocked, bot, copied, wrong-room, stale or inactive review requests receive no review reply. Outbound uncertainty remains at-most-once with no new retry.\n\n## Signed mention resolution and deliberate limitations\n\nThe existing EventSub handler checks HMAC, subscription, room and message age before `parseChat`. The parser accepts only an exact two-fragment shape: literal `!relic block ` text followed by one mention. Concatenated fragment text must equal the command exactly. Mention text and `user_login` must case-fold to the command login; `user_id` must be a bounded immutable numeric ID. Null/malformed targets, extra target fields, URLs, conflicting/duplicate mentions and prototype-like names fail closed. `user_name` is ignored as display text. The field semantics follow the parent-reviewed [Twitch channel.chat.message reference](https://dev.twitch.tv/docs/eventsub/eventsub-reference/#channel-chat-message-event).\n\nThe parser keeps an ephemeral WeakMap proof bound to the exact parsed chat object, action, room, actor and message ID. Both signed-chat store paths pass that original object into lifecycle/reduceMark, including Firestore transaction retries. Object spread, JSON/structured clones, raw action fields and a different action cannot carry the proof. Trusted service/control paths that copy an actor do not acquire mention authority. No serialized magic marker is used or trusted.\n\nResolved named blocks retain the new command's current-stream/consent/closure/freshness and reviewer checks; they are not converted into the older numeric command before those checks. Inside the transaction they use the same 128-ID bound, content removal without quota/cooldown refund, share revocation and privacy cancellation rules. Only an actual block/removal effect triggers the existing privacy fences. Completed carried associations are purged through the existing origin-mark checks. Public reply text is static and contains no target login or ID. Replay receipts still prevent a repeated message from blocking a later mentioned ID.\n\nNo login is stored in a mark, block record, cache, roster or identity index. Existing blocked IDs and existing bounded receipts remain the only durable records of this operation. Plaintext clients, multiple-fragment variants outside this deliberately narrow shape, ambiguous metadata and unavailable provider mention metadata remain unsupported and receive the honest unresolved response. Public scores, display names, configured Keeper names and previous chats are never resolution authority. No provider lookup, permission, subscription or scope is added.\n\n## Parent verification pending\n\n`test/moderator-commands.test.js` covers exact parser forms, read-only counts, pending selection, approval authority, share-grant preservation, replay/concurrency, signed memory/Firestore flows, inactive/old/expired streams, room and signature rejection, plaintext/invalid mention targets, object-copy/forgery rejection, signed structured mention success, carried-content/share/queued-reply erasure, numeric block compatibility and reply capacity. Existing marks/auto-approve/claims/privacy tests remain in place; only the exact pending acknowledgement copy and its checked-in copy snapshot are updated. Group 5B UI, general username lookup and Group 6 operations remain deferred. Only the strict signed mention shape resolves a name in this increment.
